uses: Records of licorice as a medicine reach back to ancient Assyria and Egypt, and it was traditionally given for coughs, wheezing and sore throats. Greek writers learned of the sweet root from the Scythians, and in Culpeper's day it was boiled with figs for a dry cough and hoarseness. The EMA recognizes it as a traditional remedy for heartburn-like indigestion and to loosen a cough with a cold. Grieve notes that in China it was prized as a tonic believed to keep the body young. It has long been used to hide the taste of bitter medicines, and it flavors sweets such as the Pontefract cakes made in Yorkshire.
taste: Strongly sweet, with an earthy smell
energetics: Culpeper called licorice hot and moist in temperature
caution_pregnancy: Avoid medicinal licorice in pregnancy. Large amounts of licorice are unsafe then and have been linked to birth before 38 weeks, animal studies show harm to the unborn, and the EMA advises against it in pregnancy and for women who could become pregnant and aren't using contraception. Glycyrrhizin passes into breast milk and its effect on babies is unknown, so the EMA does not recommend it while breastfeeding either.
caution_medications: Do not combine licorice with diuretics (water pills), heart medicines such as digoxin (cardiac glycosides), corticosteroids, stimulant laxatives, or other drugs that can lower potassium. It can work against blood pressure medicines. It may also change the levels of drugs broken down by the liver enzyme CYP3A4. If you take licorice medicine, avoid other licorice products as well. Talk to your provider before using it if you take any medicine.
caution_conditions: The glycyrrhizin in licorice can raise blood pressure, drop potassium and make the body hold water, and has caused irregular heartbeat and cardiac arrest. Do not use it with high blood pressure, low potassium, heart or blood vessel disease, kidney disease or liver disease; even small amounts have caused severe effects in people with these conditions or who eat a lot of salt. See a doctor if a cough brings shortness of breath, fever or phlegm containing pus. Use isn't established for anyone under 18.
caution_duration: Don't use licorice medicine for more than 4 weeks; overdose cases have come from long use or large amounts. See a practitioner if a cough lasts more than a week or indigestion more than 2 weeks. Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL), with the glycyrrhizin removed, may be safe for up to 4 months.
caution_topical: Licorice on the skin may be safe for short periods but can irritate some people's skin.
garden_harvest_timing: Leave plants for three to four years; Grieve's growers dug the roots and runners in the autumn of the fourth year, preferring plants that had never set seed.
garden_water: Deep, fertile, moist but well-drained loam or sand; does poorly on clay and dislikes salty coastal wind
notes: A perennial legume with feathery leaves and pale blue to violet pea flowers, from southeast Europe and southwest Asia. It needs a warm climate and can't take hard frost. Its deep roots and long runners make it a persistent, hard-to-remove weed once settled. Many US licorice sweets are flavored with anise oil and contain no licorice. Grieve explains the name from the Greek for sweet root, and notes that physicians since Hippocrates gave it to ease thirst. Culpeper places licorice under Mercury.
